label: Chapter 16
title: The Land of Beulah and the River

blocks.p: After this I watched until they had come into the Land of Beulah, where the sun shines night and day. Here, because they were weary, they stopped a while to rest; and because this country was common ground for pilgrims, and the orchards and vineyards here belonged to the King of the Celestial Country, they were free to help themselves to any of his things. But a little while soon refreshed them here; for the bells rang and the trumpets sounded so continually and so sweetly that they could not sleep, and yet they were as refreshed as if they had slept their sleep ever so soundly. Here, too, all the talk of those who walked in the streets was, “More pilgrims have come to town.” And another would answer, “And so many went over the water today, and were let in at the golden gates.” And again they would call, “A legion of Shining Ones has just come to town, so we know there are more pilgrims on the road; for they come here to wait for them, and to comfort them after all their sorrows.” Then the pilgrims got up and walked back and forth; and how their ears were filled now with heavenly sounds, and their eyes delighted with heavenly sights! In this land they heard nothing, saw nothing, felt nothing, smelled nothing, tasted nothing that was offensive to stomach or mind; only when they tasted the water of the river they were to cross, they found it a little bitter on the tongue, though it proved sweeter once it was down.

In this place a record was kept of the names of those who had been pilgrims in old times, and a history of all the famous deeds they had done. It was also much discussed here how the river had run high for some, and how it had ebbed while others went over. It has been nearly dry for some, while for others it has overflowed its banks.

Here the children of the town would go into the King’s gardens and gather bouquets for the pilgrims, and bring them to them with great affection. Here, too, grew camphire with spikenard, and saffron, calamus, and cinnamon, with all the trees of frankincense, myrrh, and aloes, and all the chief spices. With these the pilgrims’ rooms were perfumed while they stayed here, and with these their bodies were anointed, to prepare them to go over the river when the appointed time came.

Now, while they lay here and waited for the good hour, word went around the town that a messenger had come from the Celestial City, with business of great importance for one Christiana, the wife of Christian the pilgrim. So she was asked for, and the house where she was staying was found; and the messenger presented her with a letter. Its contents were these: “Hail, good woman! I bring you tidings that the Master calls for you, and expects you to stand in his presence, in clothes of immortality, within ten days.”

When he had read this letter to her, he gave her, along with it, a sure token that he was a true messenger, and had come to bid her make haste to be gone. The token was an arrow with a point sharpened with love, let gently into her heart, which worked on her by degrees so effectually that at the appointed time she must be gone.

When Christiana saw that her time had come, and that she was to be the first of this company to go over, she called for Mr. Great-heart, her guide, and told him how matters stood. He told her he was heartily glad of the news, and would have been glad if the messenger had come for him. Then she asked him to advise her on how everything should be prepared for her journey. So he told her: thus and thus it must be, and we who are left will go with you to the riverside.

Then she called for her children and gave them her blessing, and told them that she still read with comfort the mark that was set on their foreheads, and was glad to see them with her there, and that they had kept their garments so white. Last of all, she left to the poor the little she had, and charged her sons and her daughters to be ready for when the messenger should come for them.

When she had said these things to her guide and her children, she called for Mr. Valiant-for-truth, and said to him, “Sir, you have shown yourself true-hearted in every place. ‘Be faithful to the point of death,’ and my King will give you ‘a crown of life.’ I would also ask you to keep an eye on my children; and if at any time you see them faint, speak comfortably to them. As for my daughters, my sons’ wives, they have been faithful, and the fulfilling of the promise on them will be their end.”
But to Mr. Stand-fast she gave a ring.
Then she called for old Mr. Honest, and said of him, “’Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile.’”
“I wish you a fair day when you set out for Mount Zion,” said he, “and I shall be glad to see you go over the river dry-shod.”
But she answered, “Come wet, come dry, I long to be gone; for however the weather is on my journey, I shall have time enough when I get there to sit down and rest, and dry myself.”

Then that good man Mr. Ready-to-stumble came in to see her. She said to him, “Your travel here has been hard; but that will make your rest the sweeter. Only watch, and be ready; for the messenger may come at an hour when you are not expecting him.”

After him came Mr. Despondency and his daughter Much-afraid. To them she said, “You ought to remember with thankfulness, forever, your deliverance from the hands of Giant Despair and out of Doubting Castle. The fruit of that mercy is that you have been brought safely here. Be watchful, and cast away fear; ‘be sober, and hope to the end.’”

Then she said to Mr. Feeble-mind, “You were delivered from the mouth of Giant Slay-good so that you might live in the light of the living forever, and see your King with comfort. Only I advise you to repent of your readiness to fear, and to doubt his goodness, before he sends for you; or else when he comes you may be made to stand before him blushing for that fault.”

Now the day drew near when Christiana must be gone. So the road was full of people come to see her set out on her journey. But look: all the banks beyond the river were full of horses and chariots, come down from above to accompany her to the city gate. So she came out and entered the river, with a wave of farewell to those who had followed her to the riverside. The last words she was heard to say here were, “I come, Lord, to be with you, and to bless you.”

So her children and friends returned to their places, for those who had waited for Christiana had carried her out of their sight. And she went up and called, and entered in at the gate with all the ceremonies of joy that her husband Christian had before her.
At her departure her children wept. But Mr. Great-heart and Mr. Valiant played on the well-tuned cymbal and harp for joy. So they all went back to their own places.

In the course of time a messenger came to the town again, and his business was with Mr. Ready-to-stumble. He sought him out and said to him, “I come to you in the name of Him whom you have loved and followed, though on crutches; and my message is to tell you that he expects you at his table, to sup with him in his kingdom, the day after Easter. So prepare yourself for this journey.”
Then he also gave him a token that he was a true messenger, saying, “I have broken your golden bowl, and loosed your silver cord.” [Eccl. 12:6]

After this Mr. Ready-to-stumble called for his fellow pilgrims and told them, “I am sent for; and God will surely visit you too.” Then he asked Mr. Valiant to make his will; and because he had nothing to leave to those who would survive him except his crutches and his good wishes, he said, “These crutches I leave to my son who shall tread in my steps, with a hundred warm wishes that he may prove better than I have done.” Then he thanked Mr. Great-heart for his guidance and kindness, and set himself to his journey. When he came to the brink of the river, he said, “Now I shall have no more need of these crutches, since over there are chariots and horses for me to ride on.” The last words he was heard to say were, “Welcome, life!” So he went his way.

After this, word was brought to Mr. Feeble-mind that the messenger had sounded his horn at his chamber door. Then the messenger came in and told him, “I have come to tell you that your Master has need of you, and that in a very little while you must behold his face in brightness. And take this as a token of the truth of my message: ‘Those who look out of the windows shall be darkened.’” [Eccl. 12:3]

Then Mr. Feeble-mind called for his friends and told them what errand had been brought to him, and what token he had received of the truth of the message. Then he said, “Since I have nothing to leave to anyone, what is the point of making a will? As for my feeble mind, that I will leave behind me, for I will have no need of it in the place where I am going; nor is it worth giving to the poorest pilgrim. So when I am gone, Mr. Valiant, I ask you to bury it in a dunghill.” This done, and the day having come when he was to depart, he entered the river like the rest. His last words were, “Hold out, faith and patience.” So he went over to the other side.

When many days had passed, Mr. Despondency was sent for; a messenger had come and brought him this message: “Trembling man, this is to summon you to be ready with your King by next Lord’s Day, to shout for joy at your deliverance from all your doubtings.” And the messenger said, “To prove that my message is true, take this”: and he gave him the grasshopper to be a burden to him. [Eccl. 12:5]

Now when Mr. Despondency’s daughter, whose name was Much-afraid, heard what had happened, she said she would go with her father. Then Mr. Despondency said to his friends, “My daughter and I: you know what we have been, and how troublesome we have made ourselves in every company. My will and my daughter’s is this: that from the day of our departure, forever, our despondencies and slavish fears be received by no one; for I know that after my death they will offer themselves to others. To be plain with you, they are ghosts that we took in when we first began to be pilgrims, and we could never shake them off afterward; and they will walk about looking for lodging among the pilgrims. But for our sakes, shut the doors on them.”

When the time came for them to depart, they went to the brink of the river. The last words of Mr. Despondency were, “Farewell, night; welcome, day.” His daughter went through the river singing, but no one could understand what she said.

Then it happened, a while later, that a messenger was in the town asking for Mr. Honest. He came to the house where he was and delivered these lines into his hand: “You are commanded to be ready a week from today, to present yourself before your Lord at his Father’s house. And as a token that my message is true, ‘All the daughters of music shall be brought low.’” [Eccl. 12:4] Then Mr. Honest called for his friends and said to them, “I die, but I shall make no will. As for my honesty, it goes with me; let whoever comes after be told of this.” When the day came for him to go, he set himself to cross the river. Now at that time the river was overflowing its banks in some places; but Mr. Honest in his lifetime had spoken to one Good-conscience to meet him there, which he did, and lent him his hand, and so helped him over. The last words of Mr. Honest were, “Grace reigns.” So he left the world.

After this it was reported that Mr. Valiant-for-truth had received a summons by the same messenger as the others, and had this for a token that the summons was true: ‘that his pitcher was broken at the fountain.’ [Eccl. 12:6] When he understood it, he called for his friends and told them. “I am going to my Father’s,” he said; “and though I got here with great difficulty, I do not regret now all the trouble I went to in order to arrive where I am. My sword I give to the man who shall follow me in my pilgrimage, and my courage and skill to whoever can get them. My marks and scars I take with me, to be a witness for me that I have fought his battles, who will now be my Rewarder.” When the day came that he must go, many went with him to the riverside; and as he went into it he said, “Death, where is your sting?” And as he went down deeper, he said, “Grave, where is your victory?” So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side.

Then a summons came for Mr. Stand-fast, the one the rest of the pilgrims had found on his knees in the Enchanted Ground; the messenger brought it to him open in his hands. Its contents were that he must prepare for a change of life, for his Master was not willing that he should be so far from him any longer. At this Mr. Stand-fast fell into a muse.
“No,” said the messenger, “you need not doubt the truth of my message, for here is a token of it: ‘Your wheel is broken at the cistern.’” [Eccl. 12:6]

Then he called to him Mr. Great-heart, their guide, and said to him, “Sir, although it was not my lot to be much in your good company in the days of my pilgrimage, yet since the time I came to know you, you have done me good. When I left home, I left behind me a wife and five small children. Let me ask you, when you go back (for I know that you will go back to your Master’s house, hoping that you may yet be a guide to more of the holy pilgrims), to send to my family and let them know everything that has happened to me, or will happen. Tell them, too, of my happy arrival in this place, and of the blessed condition I am now in. Tell them also of Christian, and of Christiana his wife, and how she and her children came after her husband. Tell them what a happy end she made, and where she has gone. I have little or nothing to send my family, except prayers and tears for them; and it will be enough if you tell them of those, in case they may prevail.”

When Mr. Stand-fast had thus set things in order, and the time had come for him to hasten away, he too went down to the river. Now there was a great calm on the river at that time; so when Mr. Stand-fast was about halfway in, he stood a while and talked to the companions who had come with him there.

“This river has been a terror to many,” he said. “Yes, and the very thought of it has often frightened me. But now I find I stand easy. My foot is fixed on the place where the feet of the priests who carried the ark of the covenant stood, while Israel went over this Jordan. [Josh. 3:17] The waters are indeed bitter to the taste and cold to the stomach; yet the thought of what I am going to, and of the escort that waits for me on the other side, lies like a glowing coal at my heart.
“I see myself now at the end of my journey; my toilsome days are ended. I am going now to see the Head that was crowned with thorns, and the Face that was spat upon for me.
“I have lived until now by hearsay and faith; but now I am going where I shall live by sight, and shall be with Him in whose company I delight.
“I have loved to hear my Lord spoken of; and wherever I have seen the print of his shoe in the earth, there I have longed to set my foot too.

“His name has been to me like a box of perfume; yes, sweeter than all perfumes. His voice has been most sweet to me, and I have desired his face more than those who most desire the light of the sun. His Word I used to gather for my food, and for a remedy against my faintings. ‘He has held me, and kept me from my iniquities; yes, he has strengthened my steps in his way.’”
Now while he was speaking like this, his countenance changed; his strong man bowed under him; and after he had said, “Take me, for I come to you,” he was seen by them no more.

But glorious it was to see how the whole open region was filled with horses and chariots, with trumpeters and pipers, with singers and players on stringed instruments, to welcome the pilgrims as they went up and followed one another in at the beautiful gate of the City.

As for Christian’s children, the four boys that Christiana brought with her, with their wives and children, I did not stay where I was until they had gone over. But since I came away, I have heard it said that they are still alive, and will be for a time, for the increase of the Church in the place where they are.
Should it be my lot to go that way again, I may give those who wish it an account of what I have left unsaid here. In the meantime, I bid my reader adieu.
